drivingQuestion: What does the mishna's ruling about many and few tools teach that is not obvious?
outcomeNote: This unit is the answer to the פשיטא of the preceding unit; read alone it has no question of its own.

segments.he: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: עַד הָאִידָּנָא דַּהֲוָה לֵיהּ לְאוֹשׁוֹלֵי הֲוָה מוֹשְׁלִי לֵיהּ, הַשְׁתָּא דְּלֵיכָּא דְּמֹשֵׁיל לֵיהּ — לָא, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.
segments.en: The Gemara explains that the ruling is necessary «lest you say» that «until now, when he was» capable of «lending» one of his many adzes, if he required an additional saw someone «would lend» one «to him,» whereas «now that» his property has been repossessed «there is no» one «who will lend» such a tool «to him,» when he has nothing to offer in exchange. Consequently, the treasurer should «not» leave him with only one saw, but he should sell some of his adzes in order to purchase an additional saw. Therefore, the mishna «teaches us» that there is no concern that he might not be able to borrow a tool.

moves.summary: floats the view that a man with nothing to lend can no longer borrow, which would have made the ruling necessary
moves.about: the mishna teaches that we do not fear the impoverished craftsman will now be unable to borrow the tool he lacks

moves.summary: the mishna teaches that this concern is unfounded
moves.about: why the mishna's ruling about many and few tools is not obvious, answering the difficulty of פשיטא raised in the preceding unit
